_readme: Per-county card copy for the Watchdog county-report carousel.
FIELDS
hook  - eyebrow / short line. 5-10 words. The thing that makes this county not another county.
note  - card body. 1-2 sentences. Replaces the old generic 'Explore ... with real evidence' text.
cta   - link label.
SOURCES
Municipality counts and general tax rates: tax-rates.json (NJ Division of Taxation,
General Tax Rates by County and Municipality, 2016-2025). Rates are per $100 of
assessed value. 'Median rate' is the median across that county's municipalities for 2025.
Equalization ratios: equalization-ratios.json (Chapter 123 certification, tax year 2026).
NOTE: that file currently covers only Atlantic, Burlington, Camden, Cape May, Cumberland,
Gloucester and Salem. Ratio claims appear only in those seven entries. Do not add ratio
language to the other fourteen until the file is extended.
TWO THINGS NOT TO SAY
1. A falling tax rate is not a tax cut. Monmouth (-24% median over five years) and
Somerset (-13%) reflect revaluations resetting assessed values, not lower bills.
Their copy is written around this on purpose.
2. A high nominal rate is not a high bill. Winfield (23.411), East Brunswick (12.177)
and Kearny (10.848) are real rates on very low assessed values. Never rank counties
by rate alone without the ratio.
REFRESH
Rates change annually, usually late summer. Ratios are certified each October 1 and can
be amended by the Tax Court into the following winter. Re-derive 'note' when either file
is updated. 'hook' is durable and rarely needs to change.

atlantic.note: Atlantic County has the most consistent upward rate pressure in South Jersey, with only one municipality avoiding an increase since 2020. The spread is enormous, from Longport at 1.111 to Egg Harbor City at 5.568.

bergen.note: No county in New Jersey is more fragmented. Bergen's median rate of 2.360 hides a range from Alpine at 0.837 to Bergenfield at 3.738, and roughly half its towns held rates flat over the last five years while the other half did not.

burlington.note: Burlington's median rate is up about 12% in five years, and it is one of the broadest counties in the state at 40 municipalities. Assessment ratios run from New Hanover at 42.87 to Florence at 77.40, so two identical homes here can imply very different market values.

camden.note: At a median of 4.694 per $100, Camden County taxes harder than any of its neighbors, and Woodlynne at 8.103 is among the steepest rates in New Jersey. Pennsauken just came through a revaluation that cut its rate nearly in half and pushed its ratio to 109.7.

cape-may.note: A median rate of 1.516 sounds like relief until you see the assessments behind it. Every one of Cape May's 16 municipalities raised rates since 2020, the only county in New Jersey where that is true, and the median ratio of 51.37 means assessments here sit near half of market value.

cumberland.note: Cumberland's median ratio of 73.61 is the highest in South Jersey, which cuts both ways: less room for a Chapter 123 appeal, but also less distortion between what you are assessed at and what your home is actually worth. Bridgeton carries the county's steepest rate at 5.79.

essex.note: Essex is unusual for North Jersey in how little movement there has been, with only 13 of 22 municipalities raising rates since 2020 and a median increase of about 5%. Roseland sits at 1.862, Belleville at 4.157.

gloucester.note: Clayton assesses at 94.03 while Westville sits at 50.06, which is close to a 2x difference in how two Gloucester towns translate an assessment into implied market value. Median rate is 3.651 across 24 municipalities.

hudson.note: Hudson is the smallest county by municipality count and one of the hardest to read from rates alone. Hoboken sits at 1.805 and Kearny at 10.848, a gap that reflects assessment practice far more than it reflects anyone's actual bill.

hunterdon.note: Hunterdon has been one of the steadier counties in the state, with ten of its 26 towns holding rates level since 2020. The median sits at 2.841, with Bethlehem Township lowest at 2.021 and Milford highest at 4.027.

mercer.note: All twelve Mercer municipalities increased their general tax rate since 2020, with a median rise of about 14%. Trenton at 5.89 and Princeton at 2.733 bracket a county that has almost no low-rate options left.

middlesex.note: East Brunswick's 12.177 and Carteret's 1.568 are both real, and neither means what it looks like without the assessment ratio behind it. Middlesex's 25 municipalities have a median rate of 3.558, up roughly 11% in five years.

monmouth.note: Monmouth's median rate dropped sharply over five years, but that is revaluation resetting assessed values across the county rather than anyone's bill going down. With 53 municipalities, it is the second-largest county in the state and one where the rate is the least useful number to compare.

morris.note: Morris sits at a median rate of 2.538 with a moderate five-year climb, and its range is tighter than most large counties. Harding at 1.234 is the floor, Victory Gardens at 3.538 the ceiling.

ocean.note: Ocean County's median rate of 1.902 is among the lowest in New Jersey, and it has also climbed about 16% in five years, one of the steeper increases in the state. Shore municipalities like Mantoloking at 0.912 pull the median down without being typical of anything inland.

passaic.note: Passaic joins Cape May and Mercer as the only counties where every single municipality raised its rate since 2020. It also carries one of the highest medians in the state at 4.258, topping out with Prospect Park at 6.231.

salem.note: Salem City's 8.628 against Lower Alloway Creek's 2.004 is more than a 4x gap inside 15 municipalities. The county's median ratio of 70.08 is high by South Jersey standards, meaning assessments here already sit fairly close to market value.

somerset.note: Most Somerset municipalities show lower rates than they did in 2020, but that reflects revaluations raising assessed values rather than a genuine reduction. The county's median of 2.081 is one of the lowest in the state and one of the easiest to misread.

sussex.note: Walpack Township's 0.502 is the lowest general tax rate in the state and it sits in the same county as Hamburg at 5.135. Sussex's 24 municipalities have a median of 3.163, with about seven holding flat since 2020.

union.note: At 5.242 per $100, Union County's median general tax rate is the steepest of any New Jersey county. Winfield Township's 23.411 is a real number, driven by unusually low assessed values, and a reminder that a rate means nothing without the ratio underneath it.

warren.note: Warren has among the most uniform upward pressure in North Jersey, with a median increase of about 14% since 2020 and only one municipality holding steady. The range runs from White Township at 2.620 to Washington Borough at 5.890.
